questions.question: What is a (binary) syndrome in a linear code setting?
options: A compact vector computed from a received word that is 0 exactly when all parity checks pass
A random seed used to sample error vectors of fixed Hamming weight
A secret key component that must be kept hidden for security
A hash of the plaintext used to derive a shared secret
questions.explanation: A syndrome is the result of applying the parity-check equations; it is zero iff the word satisfies all checks.

questions.question: In the ring R = GF(2)[x]/(x^r - 1), what does reducing modulo (x^r - 1) do to exponents?
options: It wraps exponents modulo r (cyclic behavior)
It forces all polynomials to have degree exactly r
It turns multiplication into ordinary integer multiplication
It removes all odd-degree terms from the polynomial
questions.explanation: Modulo (x^r - 1) identifies x^r with 1, so exponents wrap around modulo r.

questions.question: In the toy BIKE-like model of this lesson, the syndrome is computed as:
options: s(x) = e0(x)·h0(x) + e1(x)·h1(x) in R
s(x) = h0(x)·h1(x) + e0(x)·e1(x) in R
s(x) = e0(x) + e1(x) + h0(x) + h1(x) in R
s(x) = e0(x)·e1(x) in R
questions.explanation: The syndrome is a linear image of the error under the parity-check structure: s = e0h0 + e1h1.

questions.question: In a bit-flipping decoder, what does a per-bit “counter” typically measure?
options: How many currently-unsatisfied parity checks involve that bit
The number of times the bit was sampled by the RNG
The Hamming weight of the secret key
The number of bytes in the ciphertext
questions.explanation: Counters estimate how likely a bit is wrong by correlating the current syndrome with the bit’s incident checks.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes BIKE from HQC at a high level?
options: BIKE focuses on decoding a QC-MDPC syndrome to recover a low-weight error; HQC focuses on decoding a noisy codeword using a public decodable code
BIKE is symmetric-key only; HQC is public-key only
BIKE uses only hashes; HQC uses only signatures
BIKE uses real numbers; HQC uses only prime fields
questions.explanation: Both are code-based and use QC structure, but the “decode target” differs: error/syndrome vs message/noisy codeword.

questions.question: Why can decoder failures (DFR) become a serious security issue for code-based schemes?
options: If an attacker can distinguish success vs failure (timing/errors/protocol behavior), it can act as an oracle for reaction/timing attacks
Because any nonzero DFR immediately reveals the full secret key
Because DFR only affects performance, not security
Because DFR means the hash function output is no longer uniform
questions.explanation: Even rare failures can be amplified if they are observable; distinguishing failure can leak information about the secret structure.

questions.question: What is the practical consequence of accidentally implementing polynomial multiplication modulo (x^r + 1) instead of (x^r - 1)?
options: You get a different convolution rule (negacyclic vs cyclic), so outputs and test vectors won’t match
The code becomes constant-time automatically
The ciphertext becomes shorter by a factor of 2
The decoder becomes deterministic and never fails
questions.explanation: Changing the modulus changes the ring. The sign/wrap rule differs, breaking compatibility and correctness.

questions.question: A (3,1) repetition code with majority decoding can correctly recover the bit when:
options: At most 1 of the 3 transmitted bits is flipped
At most 2 of the 3 transmitted bits are flipped
All 3 transmitted bits are flipped
Exactly 2 of the 3 transmitted bits are flipped
questions.explanation: Majority vote works as long as a strict majority remains correct, i.e., at most one bit flips in a triplet.
